facts.text: WNbMoTaV powder was ball-milled, spray-granulated using 2.5 wt.% starch at 40 wt.% solids, and spheronized in a 35 kW radiofrequency plasma under Ar/H2 flows of 70/6 L·min−1.
A 2 mm-thick preset WNbMoTaV powder layer was laser clad onto TC4 while laser power was varied from 3.1 to 3.9 kW.
The 3.3, 3.5, and 3.7 kW coatings were analyzed in detail, while the poorer-quality 3.1 and 3.9 kW coatings were excluded from detailed analysis.
Laser cladding used a 5 mm spot, 600 mm·min−1 scanning speed, 20 mm defocus, and 99.99% He shielding at 15 L·min−1.
Reciprocating wear tests used a 4 mm Si3N4 ball, 20 N load, 2 mm track, 1 Hz frequency, and 30 min duration.
Cross-sectional Vickers microhardness was measured using a 0.98 N load and a 10 s dwell.
The coatings were dense and metallurgically bonded and consisted mainly of a high-strength BCC solid solution together with a Ti-rich phase and rapid-solidification-refined grains.
BCC lattice distortion, solid-solution strengthening, and fine-grain/grain-boundary strengthening increased resistance to plastic deformation and limited plowing during sliding.
Increasing laser power reduced unfused powder and refined grains but also increased substrate dilution and formation of the Ti-rich phase; 3.5 kW gave the best balance.
During sliding, oxide formation generated a partly protective tribo-oxide layer, and coating wear was mainly oxidative with slight abrasive and adhesive contributions.
Relative to bare TC4, all detailed WNbMoTaV coatings increased hardness and wear resistance nonmonotonically, with the optimum performance at 3.5 kW.
At 3.3, 3.5, and 3.7 kW, hardness was 586.71, 670.67, and 601.22 HV0.3 and wear-volume loss was 3.28 × 10^7, 1.75 × 10^7, and 2.85 × 10^7 μm3, versus 341.25 HV0.3 and 6.09 × 10^7 μm3 for bare TC4.
